tEn: Sam Altman on AI, Superintelligence & the Future of Humanity
tZh: Sam Altman 谈 AI、超级智能与人类未来
sEn: Sam Altman opens up about building superintelligence, the personal cost of a crazy life, and why India is AI's biggest optimist.
sZh: Sam Altman 坦陈打造超级智能的代价、身处疯狂生活的感受，以及为何印度对 AI 最为乐观。

consensus.en: Scaling neural networks yields super-linear returns; this intuition predated scaling laws and drove OpenAI's big compute bet.
consensus.zh: 扩大神经网络规模会带来超线性回报；这一直觉早于缩放定律，并推动了 OpenAI 的算力豪赌。

consensus.en: Launching early, even if embarrassing, is crucial for feedback; a small group of passionate users beats many lukewarm ones.
consensus.zh: 尽早发布，即使产品令人尴尬，对获取反馈至关重要；一小群狂热用户胜过许多不温不火的用户。

consensus.en: Surround yourself with smart people and mostly listen to them; going against all advice should be rare and high-stakes.
consensus.zh: 让自己身边围绕聪明人，并大多听从他们；违背所有建议应该是罕见且高风险的。

consensus.en: The best time in history to build a company; AI enables extraordinary new products and startups worldwide.
consensus.zh: 这是历史上创办公司的最佳时机；AI 在全球范围内催生了非凡的新产品和初创公司。

consensus.en: A great research lab culture combines high conviction on the mission with open-minded exploration everywhere else.
consensus.zh: 伟大的研究实验室文化将使命上的高度信念与其他方面的开放探索相结合。

consensus.en: Compounding in careers requires continuously pushing into uncomfortable, non-obvious new challenges; most people stop early.
consensus.zh: 职业生涯中的复利需要不断推动自己进入不舒服、非显而易见的新挑战；大多数人很早就停止了。

contrarian.en: Being misunderstood by most people is a strength if you're right; short-term low status can be traded for long-term high status.
contrarian.zh: 如果你是对的，被大多数人误解是一种优势；短期低地位可以换取长期高地位。

contrarian.en: Most advice is terrible; founders should listen to less advice and figure things out on their own.
contrarian.zh: 大多数建议都很糟糕；创始人应该少听建议，自己摸索。

contrarian.en: You can teach people to become more ambitious through peer groups and successive challenges, contrary to the belief it's innate.
contrarian.zh: 你可以通过同伴群体和 successive 挑战教会人们变得更有野心，这与认为野心是天生的观点相反。

contrarian.en: AI development should be pluralistic; multiple competing efforts with different approaches are safer than one dominant player.
contrarian.zh: AI 发展应该是多元的；多个采用不同方法的竞争性努力比一个主导者更安全。

contrarian.en: Not having equity in OpenAI was a mistake; it confuses people because it's outside the norm of business motivations.
contrarian.zh: 在 OpenAI 不持有股权是一个错误；这让人困惑，因为它超出了商业动机的常规。

contrarian.en: The US is unusually negative on AI relative to the rest of the world, especially developing countries like India.
contrarian.zh: 相对于世界其他地区，尤其是像印度这样的发展中国家，美国对 AI 异常消极。

turns.en: Before we start today's episode, I just have one request. Please subscribe to our channel. Me and my team work every day and try to bring the most valuable conversations from the world. All we want in return is just one subscribe from you.
turns.zh: 在我们开始今天的节目之前，我有一个请求。请订阅我们的频道。我和我的团队每天都在努力，试图带来世界上最有价值的对话。我们想要的回报只是你的一个订阅。

turns.en: On Figuring Out, we try to study how the world's most extraordinary minds think, and that's exactly what today's episode is about. Today's episode with Sam Altman is not about AI, it's not about technology, it's about a human being who's building that technology. What are his insecurities? What are his fears? How does he think as a friend, as a father, as someone who's trying to build one of the most important things which will shape humanity? How does he notice patterns and find the non-obvious things to work on to build something incredible in the future? That's what we've tried to understand. I hope by the end of the podcast, you get to extract some lessons from his mind and implement in your life to make your life better. Watch this episode and let me know in the comments how did you find it. And the styling partner for this episode is Levis. Click on the link in the description to explore their latest collection. Enjoy the show.
turns.zh: 在《Figuring Out》节目中，我们试图研究世界上最非凡的头脑是如何思考的，而这正是今天这集的内容。今天与 Sam Altman 的这集不是关于 AI，不是关于技术，而是关于一个正在构建那项技术的人。他的不安全感是什么？他的恐惧是什么？作为朋友、作为父亲、作为试图构建将塑造人类的最重要事物之一的人，他是如何思考的？他如何注意到模式并找到非显而易见的事情去努力，在未来构建出不可思议的东西？这就是我们试图理解的。我希望在播客结束时，你能从他的头脑中提取一些经验教训，并应用到你的生活中，让你的生活更美好。观看这集节目，并在评论中告诉我你觉得如何。本集的造型合作伙伴是 Levis。点击描述中的链接探索他们的最新系列。享受节目吧。

turns.en: Welcome on the show, Sam. Welcome on Figuring Out. It's an honor.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到节目，Sam。欢迎来到《Figuring Out》。很荣幸。

turns.en: I really appreciate you doing this.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你这样做。

turns.en: You know, if someone's watching you for the first time and they have no clue who you are, how would you explain to them who you are in the next 60 seconds?
turns.zh: 你知道，如果有人第一次看你，完全不知道你是谁，你会如何在接下来的 60 秒内向他们解释你是谁？

turns.en: Um, I'm like a tech fan, like a curious person about the world and a believer that AI is going to be this thing that touches all of our lives, hopefully in mostly super positive ways. Um, I'm a dad. I really love my kids. That's what I would say.
turns.zh: 嗯，我像个技术迷，对世界充满好奇，并且相信 AI 将成为触及我们所有人生活的事物，希望主要以非常积极的方式。嗯，我是一位父亲。我非常爱我的孩子。这就是我想说的。

turns.en: But do you ever think about certain things that this is how you're going to think or say or speak about?
turns.zh: 但你是否曾想过某些事情，比如这就是你思考或说话的方式？

turns.en: Um, I do just kind of try to naturally talk about what's on my mind, uh, or what I'm interested in.
turns.zh: 嗯，我只是试着自然地谈论我脑子里想的事情，或者我感兴趣的事情。

turns.en: Okay. And were you like this since you were a kid, always thinking about what interesting to say next?
turns.zh: 好的。你从小就是这样吗，总是想着接下来要说什么有趣的话？

turns.en: Cuz I think I was like that as a kid. I think I would just try to like I think I just always followed what I was curious about.
turns.zh: 因为我觉得我小时候就是那样。我想我只是试着……我觉得我一直追随我好奇的东西。

turns.en: And do you as a kid did you ever feel inferior to someone?
turns.zh: 你小时候有没有觉得不如别人？

turns.en: All the time? I mean, I'm sure most kids do. Uh, but I was like, you know, I was like a very nerdy kid. I like wasn't good at sports and I grew up at a time when like that was the very much the cool thing.
turns.zh: 一直都有？我是说，我确信大多数孩子都会。嗯，但我就像，你知道，我是个非常书呆子的孩子。我不擅长运动，而我成长的时代，那恰恰是很酷的事情。

turns.en: Same.
turns.zh: 一样。

turns.en: Uh, yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的。

turns.en: I was not good at sports either.
turns.zh: 我也不擅长运动。

turns.en: And it was like the cool thing.
turns.zh: 而那却是很酷的事情。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. Um, so yeah, total. I was like not a— I was not— I always had like a lot of friends and I connected well with people, but I was never like a cool kid.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，所以是的，完全如此。我就像不是——我不是——我一直有很多朋友，我和人们相处得很好，但我从来不是那种酷小孩。

turns.en: Okay. Did that bother you?
turns.zh: 好的。那让你困扰吗？

turns.en: Sort of. Um, I mean, it did not like— I don't think it bothered me like it bothers some people, but yeah, I think all kids like want to be popular and cool and there's like— I think it's like very painful as a kid to not feel like in the inner circle or whatever.
turns.zh: 有一点。嗯，我是说，它没有像——我不认为它像困扰某些人那样困扰我，但是的，我认为所有孩子都想受欢迎和酷，而且就像——我觉得对孩子来说，感觉不在核心圈子里什么的，是非常痛苦的。

turns.en: You said it didn't bother you as it would to some people. What do you mean by that? Well, what's the distinction? What did you think about?
turns.zh: 你说它没有像对某些人那样困扰你。你是什么意思？嗯，区别是什么？你怎么想的？

turns.en: I've talked to other people who are like, 'Ah, you know, the defining characteristic of my childhood was that I was like a nerd and not cool and I hated that.' And I was like, 'I was a nerd and not cool and it like slightly bothered me, but I had my computer and I had like my little core set of friends and I, you know, like I had a wonderful childhood and I think I was like very happy.'
turns.zh: 我和其他人聊过，他们会说：‘啊，你知道，我童年的决定性特征就是我像个书呆子，不酷，我讨厌那样。’而我会说：‘我是个书呆子，不酷，这有点困扰我，但我有我的电脑，我有我的小核心朋友圈，而且我，你知道，我有一个美好的童年，我觉得我非常快乐。’

turns.en: Okay. So, here's what I want to do. I want to talk more about your brain, like how you think, how you actually make decisions, and what you think about certain things because I think that's really fascinating to me.
turns.zh: 好的。所以，我想做的是，我想多谈谈你的大脑，比如你如何思考，你实际上如何做决定，以及你对某些事情的看法，因为我觉得那对我来说真的很有趣。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: And it's great— underexplored.
turns.zh: 而且这很棒——未被充分探索。

turns.en: I think it's really hard to like talk about yourself this way, but I'll try my best.
turns.zh: 我觉得这样谈论自己真的很难，但我会尽力。

turns.en: Yeah. Maybe just the kind of things you— because you've said a couple of things in like a lot of your interviews here and there and I don't know why people didn't just go like deep down on that alley. Something I want to do.
turns.zh: 是的。也许只是那些事情——因为你在很多采访中零零散散地说过一些事情，我不知道为什么人们没有深入那条路。这是我想做的。

turns.en: So what version of you has died? Like who were you when you started and who have you become?
turns.zh: 那么你的哪个版本已经消失了？比如你开始时是谁，现在你变成了谁？

turns.en: Um, I was like much more carefree. Like when we started OpenAI, I was just like, you know, I had a very easy life at the time. I had a lot of hobbies and you know now I'm like incredibly precisely scheduled and I have not gotten to do anything spontaneous in a long time.
turns.zh: 嗯，我那时更无忧无虑。比如当我们创办 OpenAI 时，我就像，你知道，我当时生活很轻松。我有很多爱好，而现在我就像被极其精确地安排，我已经很久没有做过任何即兴的事情了。

turns.en: Was there any point ever in your life where nobody else was convinced but just you?
turns.zh: 你生活中是否有过这样的时刻：除了你，没有人相信？

turns.en: Launching ChatGPT was kind of an example of that. Not that people didn't want to launch a chatbot, but most people thought it was too early and not good enough.
turns.zh: 推出 ChatGPT 就是一个例子。并不是人们不想推出聊天机器人，而是大多数人认为为时过早，还不够好。

turns.en: When you talk to other people, do they tell you that you're delusional sometimes?
turns.zh: 当你和其他人交谈时，他们有时会告诉你你是在妄想吗？

turns.en: Yes, but I think I should probably get more of that.
turns.zh: 是的，但我觉得我可能应该得到更多这样的反馈。

turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: Well, one way that like a lot of people in roles like mine have had things go wrong is they get surrounded by too many yes-men.
turns.zh: 嗯，很多像我这样角色的人出问题的一个方式就是他们被太多的唯唯诺诺者包围。

turns.en: You've gone through like people suing you, people dropping out. There's government like trying to find out so many things about you. Have you changed as a person with all of this now?
turns.zh: 你经历了人们起诉你，人们退出。政府试图了解关于你的很多事情。经历了这一切，你作为一个人改变了吗？

turns.en: There's no way that anyone was going to like get to build superintelligence and not have a crazy life, but I think I'm kind of like well-wired for it. Like I can deal with a lot of insanity whipping around me.
turns.zh: 任何人想要构建超级智能，都不可能没有疯狂的生活，但我觉得我天生适合这个。就像我能应对周围很多疯狂的事情。

transcript.sec: AI Optimism in India vs US

turns.en: When I talk to somebody in US, they're slightly pessimistic about AI. And when I talk to people in India, they're very optimistic about it.
turns.zh: 当我和美国的人交谈时，他们对 AI 有点悲观。而当我与印度的人交谈时，他们非常乐观。

turns.en: It's an incredible difference. India is like our biggest market in the world.
turns.zh: 这是一个不可思议的差异。印度就像我们在世界上最大的市场。

turns.en: Why do you think it's the difference?
turns.zh: 你认为为什么会有这种差异？

turns.en: One thing that countries that are developing faster where the economy is growing faster and there's like more of a need for products and services and are more welcoming of AI than more developed economies. So, I'm sure that's part of it.
turns.zh: 一个原因是，发展更快的国家，经济增长更快，对产品和服务有更多需求，并且比更发达的经济体更欢迎 AI。所以，我确信这是部分原因。

transcript.secZh: 印度与美国的AI乐观主义

turns.en: Do you think you're still being misunderstood today?
turns.zh: 你认为你今天仍然被误解吗？

turns.en: This technology is still not very well understood, but I think people at least understand AI is happening worldwide. This is like certainly the best time I've ever seen to make a new company.
turns.zh: 这项技术仍然没有被很好地理解，但我认为人们至少明白 AI 正在全世界发生。这无疑是我见过的最好的创办新公司的时机。

turns.en: Do you worry about it, OpenAI?
turns.zh: 你担心 OpenAI 吗？

turns.en: Yeah, of course.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。

turns.en: What's your biggest worry?
turns.zh: 你最大的担忧是什么？

turns.en: We have done something. We will continue to do something that is going to be an extraordinary force in society. I believe it can be a force for good. But you know it's like very high stakes and we have like a lot of responsibility.
turns.zh: 我们已经做了一些事情。我们将继续做一些将成为社会中非凡力量的事情。我相信它可以成为一股向善的力量。但你知道，这风险极高，我们肩负着很多责任。

turns.en: Do you feel that when you're gone you're not there to guide or protect your kids or family? Would you be very comfortable your kids growing up in AI powered world which you're helping create today?
turns.zh: 你是否觉得当你离开后，你不在那里指导或保护你的孩子或家人？你会很放心你的孩子在你今天帮助创造的 AI 驱动的世界中成长吗？

turns.en: You know when I talk to somebody in the US, a random person, they're slightly pessimistic about AI. And when I talk to people in India, they're very optimistic about it.
turns.zh: 你知道，当我和美国随便一个人聊起 AI 时，他们多少有点悲观。而我和印度人聊时，他们非常乐观。

turns.en: It's an incredible difference.
turns.zh: 这差异令人难以置信。

turns.en: Why do you think it's the difference?
turns.zh: 你觉得为什么会有这种差异？

turns.en: Well, first of all, India is like our biggest market in the world by touch users and growing very quickly. And there's incredible builder energy of people using it.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，按触达用户数算，印度大概是我们全球最大的市场，而且增长非常快。那里有令人难以置信的构建者能量，人们都在使用它。

turns.en: Bigger than US?
turns.zh: 比美国还大？

turns.en: Yeah, more just India than the US. And I mean people are just using it in incredible ways to build companies. Or you know, I just heard about some Indian kid that needed to do some fundraising for his school and had never done fundraising before, and was able to get the full stack of it done with a set of our tools, and it was awesome. So I think it's a country that has a lot of adoption. It's growing very quickly. But I do think that the US, at least on expressed preference, is unusually negative on AI relative to the rest of the world, and India is maybe unusually positive.
turns.zh: 是的，印度比美国更大。人们正以令人难以置信的方式使用它来创办公司。比如我刚听说有个印度孩子需要为学校筹款，他以前从未做过筹款，但用我们的一套工具就把整个流程都搞定了，太棒了。所以我认为这是一个采用率很高的国家，增长非常快。但我确实认为，至少从表达出的偏好来看，美国对 AI 的态度相对于世界其他地方异常负面，而印度可能异常积极。

turns.en: But why? Like what do you make out of it? Why is it? Why there's difference?
turns.zh: 但为什么？你怎么看？为什么会有这种差异？

turns.en: One thing that many people have observed is that countries that are developing faster, where the economy is growing faster and there's more of a need for products and services and there's just huge under supply, are more welcoming of AI than more developed economies. So I'm sure that's part of it.
turns.zh: 很多人观察到的一点是，发展更快的国家，经济增长更快，对产品和服务的需求更大，供应严重不足，这些国家比更发达的经济体更欢迎 AI。所以我确信这是部分原因。

turns.en: Interesting. And the other thing when I read about you, right, like I read about you in US and I read about you in India, this sentiment of being pessimistic and optimistic, it also reflects about you. And that's the most fascinating thing that you're this person who started this most remarkable technological revolution here of our age. You were the first guy. You don't even own equity in your own company. And yet all of a sudden you became the bad guy. Like how? Why?
turns.zh: 有意思。另外，当我在美国读到关于你的报道，在印度读到关于你的报道，这种悲观和乐观的情绪也反映了你。最引人注目的是，你是我们这个时代最非凡的技术革命的发起者。你是第一人。你甚至不持有自己公司的股权。然而突然间你成了坏人。怎么会？为什么？

turns.en: Well, I think the US has great skepticism of people in power and in particular of the just enormous power that the tech industry holds. But you know, I would say like this is probably a good thing in some ways. It does feel to me like it's gone a little far.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为美国对掌权者有着强烈的怀疑，尤其是对科技行业所掌握的庞大权力。但你知道，我想说这在某些方面可能是件好事。不过我觉得它有点过头了。

turns.en: Interesting. What do you think is the biggest misunderstanding about you in the world?
turns.zh: 有意思。你认为世界上对你最大的误解是什么？

turns.en: Well, you touched on one of them, but I think not taking—not having equity in OpenAI has been a mistake. I did it for what I thought were good reasons. I think it's just been hugely confusing to people. It's kind of interesting to me, right? If an artist works super hard on their art project or a sports star practices super hard and doesn't make a ton of money from it, no one has a problem with that. That's kind of understood. And this is like my equivalent of that. But yeah, it's been—
turns.zh: 嗯，你提到了其中一个，但我认为不持有 OpenAI 股权是个错误。我这么做是出于我认为正当的理由。我觉得这让人非常困惑。这对我来说挺有意思的，对吧？如果一个艺术家非常努力地做艺术项目，或者一个体育明星非常努力地训练，但没有从中赚很多钱，没人会觉得有问题。这是可以理解的。这就像我的对应版本。但没错，这一直——

turns.en: Why is it misunderstood? What do people not like? What do they not get about it?
turns.zh: 为什么会被误解？人们不喜欢什么？他们不理解什么？

turns.en: I think it's just very outside of the norm of why people assume that people start companies or work as business people.
turns.zh: 我认为这完全超出了人们假设人们创办公司或作为商人工作的常规原因。

turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.en: It's just weird. And people don't like weird.
turns.zh: 就是很奇怪。人们不喜欢奇怪的东西。

turns.en: People don't like weird.
turns.zh: 人们不喜欢奇怪的东西。

turns.en: It's weird to me as well.
turns.zh: 对我来说也很奇怪。

turns.en: Yeah. And then you're like, well, why is he really doing it? Is it about, you know?
turns.zh: 是啊。然后你就会想，他到底为什么这么做？是为了，你知道？

turns.en: And why you doing it?
turns.zh: 那你为什么这么做？

turns.en: I think this is the most interesting work and kind of the most important and useful thing I can imagine doing. It's incredibly interesting. It's incredibly exciting to get to do. Like, I mean, what a quest.
turns.zh: 我认为这是我能想象到的最有趣的工作，也是最有用的事情。它极其有趣。能做这件事太令人兴奋了。我的意思是，多么伟大的探索。

turns.en: True. But it's a rabbit hole we'll just keep going into because I don't understand this at all just like a lot of other people. But I really respect what you do. So thank you.
turns.zh: 确实。但这是一个我们会一直深入下去的兔子洞，因为我和许多其他人一样完全不明白。但我真的很尊重你所做的事。所以谢谢你。

turns.en: Okay. One of the things you said—I'll read it exactly as it is—that you should trade being short-term low status for being long-term high status. Which most people seem unwilling to do. Right? So, as long as you're right, being misunderstood by most people is a strength, not weakness. I find it fascinating. But the question is how, before the outcome is clear, how do you know that this is being misunderstood and this not being wrong?
turns.zh: 好的。你说过的一件事——我照原话读——你应该用短期的低地位换取长期的高地位。大多数人似乎不愿意这么做。对吧？所以，只要你是对的，被大多数人误解是一种优势，而不是弱点。我觉得这很迷人。但问题是，在结果明朗之前，你怎么知道这是被误解而不是错了？

turns.en: Well, the hard part is you don't really know. You can have a high degree of conviction. You can have an increasing degree of conviction as you get more evidence, which I think is the right thing to go for, but you don't know for sure. That's part of the excitement—that you don't know for sure. But when we first started OpenAI, it was an extremely low status thing to do. We knew it'd be valuable if we get it to work, but almost no one took us seriously. It was like, okay, AGI, maybe 100 years from now, maybe never. You're a bunch of kids and you don't have the polished academics and whatever, and very, very negative. We had a reason to make the bet, and as we figured more things out, we had a reason to be more confident, but it's still kind of amazing it all worked. So I think it was a good expected value bet to take, but it was far, far, far from certain.
turns.zh: 嗯，难就难在你并不真正知道。你可以有高度的信念。随着证据增多，你的信念可以越来越强，我认为这是正确的做法，但你无法确定。这也是兴奋的一部分——你无法确定。但当我们刚创办 OpenAI 时，那是地位极低的事情。我们知道如果成功会有价值，但几乎没人把我们当回事。就像，好吧，AGI，也许 100 年后，也许永远不会。你们是一群孩子，没有光鲜的学术背景什么的，非常非常负面。我们有理由下这个赌注，随着我们弄明白更多事情，我们有理由更自信，但这一切能成功仍然有点神奇。所以我认为这是一个值得下的期望值赌注，但远非确定。

turns.en: But what were the signals that made you very certain that this might work? This something that I want to do.
turns.zh: 但什么信号让你非常确定这可能行得通？这是我想做的事。

turns.en: Yeah. I kind of think all of us get a small number of great insights over our lives that we apply again and again in new ways. And one of them for me was the surprising properties of scale. I noticed this in companies, countries, cities, individual people's careers, lots of pieces of technology, networks like Y Combinator, which was the thing I was doing before. When you really scale up something that's working at small scale, you often see big super linear returns to doing it at bigger scale. And because, like anybody else, I'm a pattern matcher whether I mean to do it or not. Once we saw that neural networks were working at all and they were getting better with scale, I was very interested and I had a strong intuition that we should try to scale them up a lot more. Now this was before we knew how precisely we could predict properties with scale. This was years before we had the scaling laws. But we had this observation approximately that if you made a neural network bigger it could do more impressive things, and this had first led to the AlexNet result and then many more things after. But then these were the signals—probably a lot of people must be seeing, right? What was preventing them to build on it?
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得我们一生中都会获得少量伟大的洞见，然后以新的方式反复应用。对我来说，其中之一就是 Scaling（规模扩张）的惊人特性。我在公司、国家、城市、个人职业生涯、许多技术、像 Y Combinator 这样的网络中都注意到了这一点，那是我之前在做的事。当你真正扩大在小规模下有效的东西时，你常常会看到在大规模下做这件事会带来巨大的超线性回报。而且像任何人一样，不管我是否有意，我都是一个模式匹配者。一旦我们看到神经网络开始起作用，并且随着规模扩大而变得更好，我就非常感兴趣，并且有强烈的直觉认为我们应该尝试将它们扩大得多得多。这是在我们可以精确预测规模特性之前。这是在缩放定律出现几年前。但我们大致观察到，如果你把神经网络做得更大，它就能做更令人印象深刻的事情，这首先导致了 AlexNet 的结果，然后之后还有更多。但这些信号——可能很多人都看到了，对吧？是什么阻止了他们在此基础上发展？

turns.en: I find this one of the most confusing things I have ever observed in my career. Why in 2015, 2016 and then even by 2018 to 2021, why other people were looking at the same data and not saying this is crazy, like we have to invest much more in this.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是我职业生涯中观察到的最令人困惑的事情之一。为什么在 2015 年、2016 年，甚至到 2018 到 2021 年，为什么其他人看着同样的数据，却没有说这太疯狂了，我们必须在这上面投入更多。

turns.en: It seemed so obvious to me and everybody else in the building. I mean, maybe we felt delusional because we were like, how can anybody not see this? I think there was something about it that almost felt too easy. It almost felt too unfathomable. You'd look at the mistakes that these neural networks were making and you would say, there's no way that something so dumb can just fix all of its problems by scaling it up. It seemed like all these smart people were saying you have to have symbolic representations or you have to do this, or I can give you this very good reason.
turns.zh: 在我看来，这栋楼里的其他人也都觉得这显而易见。我的意思是，也许我们觉得自己有点妄想，因为我们想，怎么可能有人看不到这一点？我觉得这件事几乎让人觉得太容易了。几乎让人觉得太不可思议了。你看着这些神经网络犯的错误，你会说，这么笨的东西不可能仅仅通过扩大规模就解决所有问题。似乎所有聪明人都在说，你必须要有符号表示，或者你必须这样做，或者我可以给你一个非常好的理由。

turns.en: I remember someone articulating why our approach was never going to work and it sounded so convincing.
turns.zh: 我记得有人阐述了为什么我们的方法永远行不通，听起来非常有说服力。

turns.en: What was it?
turns.zh: 是什么？

turns.en: It went something like: all right, what these models are doing is they are learning to predict from what's in their training set what's likely to come next. But that means they're never going to be able to make new knowledge because they can only model what's in their training set. And that sounds very reasonable. Maybe you can show a model a million math problems and it can learn how to do those math problems, but you didn't show it a new thing that wasn't yet proven because it wasn't yet known, and so it wasn't going to be able to do that. And obviously now we know that's ridiculous. But at the time it sounded very compelling. And the thing that it was missing is that what these models are learning is not—I mean, also is—but the important thing they're learning is not these specific math problems but the general-purpose ability of reasoning, and that can expand into new things.
turns.zh: 大概是这样的：这些模型所做的是，它们学习从训练集中的内容预测接下来可能是什么。但这意味着它们永远无法创造新知识，因为它们只能对训练集中的内容建模。这听起来非常合理。也许你可以给模型看一百万道数学题，它可以学会如何做这些数学题，但你没有给它看一个尚未被证明的新事物，因为那还不为人所知，所以它无法做到。显然现在我们知道那是荒谬的。但当时听起来非常有说服力。它忽略的是，这些模型学到的不是——我的意思是，也是——但重要的是，它们学到的不是这些具体的数学题，而是通用的推理能力，而这种能力可以扩展到新事物。

turns.en: So take me to a specific decision when you were doing all of this and other people were telling you that hey this might never work out right. Tell me to one take me to one consequential decision that you took with 50% certainty and 50% delusion.
turns.zh: 那么，带我回到一个具体的决定，当时你在做所有这些事情，而其他人告诉你，嘿，这可能永远不会成功。告诉我一个你带着 50% 确定性和 50% 妄想做出的重大决定。

turns.en: After we finished training GPT-4. This was about, I think it was August of 2022.
turns.zh: 在我们完成训练 GPT-4 之后。大约是在 2022 年 8 月。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: And we finished it about seven or eight months before we released it to the world. Something like that. But we were sitting on it and we were looking at it and we knew it was extraordinary. But it took us a little while to realize just like the new avenues of research this was going to open up and how quickly the models were likely to improve post GPT-4 and that we could do what became the chain of thought work and the reasoning models. And we then decided we were going to go make a very big bet on compute because we saw that we could continue to scale models and that the value of these models would be really important. But it was new and the rest of the world wasn't there yet. They hadn't even seen GPT-4. They had not internalized what we thought it could do. And so we decided we would bet the company on buying up a lot of compute. And that felt very crazy to people. But we had enough conviction that we were probably right because we were able to use this model and we had internalized the scaling properties.
turns.zh: 我们在向世界发布它之前大约七八个月完成了训练。差不多是这样。但我们当时按兵不动，我们看着它，我们知道它非同寻常。但我们花了一点时间才意识到这将开辟的新研究途径，以及 GPT-4 之后模型可能改进的速度，还有我们可以做后来成为思维链工作和推理模型的事情。然后我们决定在算力上押下非常大的赌注，因为我们看到我们可以继续扩展模型，而这些模型的价值将非常重要。但这是新事物，世界其他地方还没跟上。他们甚至还没见过 GPT-4。他们还没有内化我们认为它能做的事情。所以我们决定把公司押在购买大量算力上。这对人们来说显得非常疯狂。但我们有足够的信念，认为我们可能是对的，因为我们能够使用这个模型，而且我们已经内化了 Scaling（规模扩张）的特性。

turns.en: And what was the other option? You had a much less ambitious bet on compute and a slower rate of scaling.
turns.zh: 那另一个选择是什么？你有一个雄心小得多的算力赌注和更慢的 Scaling（规模扩张）速度。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And do you think if any amount of other information you would have gotten at that point, you would have changed the decision?
turns.zh: 你认为如果当时你获得任何其他信息，你会改变决定吗？

turns.en: I think if the model were even a little bit less smart, you know, if GPT-4 had come out at like the GPT-3.8 scale, we would not have had the conviction to do such a big bet.
turns.zh: 我认为如果模型哪怕稍微不那么聪明，你知道，如果 GPT-4 出来时只有 GPT-3.8 的规模，我们就不会有信念去做这么大的赌注。

turns.en: When you talk to other people, do they tell you that you're delusional sometimes even today?
turns.zh: 当你和其他人交谈时，他们有时甚至今天还会告诉你你在妄想吗？

turns.en: Yes, but I think I should probably get more of that.
turns.zh: 是的，但我认为我可能应该得到更多这样的反馈。

turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: Well, I think one way that a lot of people in roles like mine have had things go wrong is they get surrounded by too many yes-men. And you really need the pushback.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为很多像我这样角色的人出问题的一个方式是，他们被太多的唯唯诺诺者包围。你真的需要有人反驳你。

turns.en: But how do you make sure that today you are not surrounded with yes men?
turns.zh: 但你怎么确保今天你没有被唯唯诺诺者包围？

turns.en: Having your old friends around is very helpful. Having people that you've worked with for, you know, 10 plus years is very useful. And then really cultivating a culture where you reward people for pushing back hard when you're wrong and making that easy to do. I think is also important. But it takes active care. You know, the more times that you've been right and the more sort of power in the world you have, I think the harder this is to get.
turns.zh: 让老朋友在身边非常有帮助。有和你共事过 10 多年的人非常有用。然后真正培养一种文化，当你错了时，奖励那些大力反驳你的人，并让这样做变得容易。我认为这也很重要。但这需要主动的关怀。你知道，你越多次正确，你在世界上拥有的权力越大，我认为这越难获得。

turns.en: See, here's the confusion as a founder. So when you have like all old friends, really smart people, the mentors that you think about, you have them around you and they're telling you that, hey, this is wrong and you're thinking in the wrong direction. How do you then convince them or probably just go against them? And how do you know that going against them is the right thing today? Because I'm sure this happens.
turns.zh: 看，作为创始人，这里有个困惑。所以当你身边都是老朋友、非常聪明的人、你想到的导师，你让他们在你身边，他们告诉你，嘿，这是错的，你在往错误的方向思考。那你如何说服他们，或者可能只是违背他们？你今天怎么知道违背他们是对的？因为我确信这会发生。

turns.en: The number of times that I do something against everyone else's advice is very small. It happens, but it's rare. And I have met some people, and founders in particular, who take the most pride in doing something when everyone else tells them it's wrong. And my own belief is you should only do that very grudgingly. If you surround yourself by smart people, you should mostly listen to them. And if you decide that even though none of them think what you're doing is the right thing to do and you're going to do it anyway, you should view that as an expensive, unlikely to be right, high-stakes thing. And you really want to have conviction on that.
turns.zh: 我违背所有人建议做事的次数非常少。会发生，但很罕见。我遇到过一些人，尤其是创始人，他们最自豪的是在所有人都告诉他们错了的时候做某事。我自己的信念是，你应该非常不情愿地这样做。如果你身边都是聪明人，你应该 mostly 听他们的。如果你决定，即使他们都不认为你做的事是对的，你还是要做，你应该把这看作一件代价高昂、不太可能正确、高风险的事情。你真的需要对那有信念。

turns.en: And talking about smart people and other founders, what do you think? What stops them? They're intelligent, clearly intelligent. What stops them to build such extraordinary things like you've done?
turns.zh: 谈到聪明人和其他创始人，你怎么看？是什么阻止了他们？他们很聪明，显然很聪明。是什么阻止他们建立像你所做的这样非凡的东西？

turns.en: Well, I think AI has happened only once. So, I think we got lucky or did a good job or whatever on problem selection. But I think a lot of people build extraordinary things. The rate of great companies being created right now, I have never seen it be so high worldwide. I think this is certainly the best time I've ever seen. I believe it is probably the best time in history to be able to build something, to make a new company, to make a new technology, to make a new kind of creative project. We have just gotten this unbelievable gift and I think it's incredible what people are doing right now. So, I think we're going to see a lot of very extraordinary things—companies and otherwise—get built.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为 AI 只发生过一次。所以，我认为我们在问题选择上运气好或做得好或其他什么。但我认为很多人建立了非凡的东西。现在伟大公司被创造的速度，我从未见过全世界范围内这么高。我认为这无疑是我见过的最好的时代。我相信这可能是历史上建立某样东西、创建新公司、创造新技术、创造新类型创意项目的最好时机。我们刚刚得到了这份难以置信的礼物，我认为人们现在做的事情令人难以置信。所以，我认为我们将看到很多非常非凡的东西——公司和其他——被建立起来。

turns.en: So now that everyone's building companies and there are so many things happening, the action is happening, some founders watching this right now are thinking that things that are obvious to me because of AI and technology are not obvious to a lot of people. How can that person judge that it's the right thing to do and it's not being misunderstood?
turns.zh: 现在每个人都在创业，有太多事情在发生，行动正在进行。有些正在观看的创始人会想，因为 AI 和技术，对我来说显而易见的事情，对很多人来说并不明显。那个人如何判断这是正确的事情，并且没有被误解？

turns.en: I mean, this is kind of what you get paid to do as a founder, right? This is where if you are starting the most ambitious company you could start, you'll certainly be misunderstood.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这有点像你作为创始人应该做的事，对吧？如果你要创办你能创办的最有雄心的公司，你肯定会被人误解。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Now, there are many other companies that are obviously good ideas and you can still succeed big time at those, but if the ideas are obvious, a lot of other ambitious people are going to start them, too. So when we started OpenAI in 2015, I think you could count on one hand the number of AGI labs that were being started that year. I mean, maybe you could count it on much less than one hand. Maybe it was only OpenAI that year. I'm not sure. And yet there were probably like 10,000 photo sharing companies. Most people thought starting a photo sharing company was a better idea. But the problem is there were 10,000 others and also Instagram had a big network effect and whatever else. So I think picking things that you have a reason to believe are more valuable than they seem, even if they're unlikely to work. So valuable if they work that the expected value is good. You have a real advantage when you find something like that. When you understand a technology or a piece of science or something about the world before other people do, there's some instinct which I understand to say, 'Ah, you know, there's all these smart people and I don't want them to call me dumb, so they don't get it and they're going to talk me out of it.' But I think there's another instinct which I encourage people to cultivate, which is if you really understand something and it's not just wishful thinking, but you can articulate why it's a good bet, you should cherish those moments. Like that's awesome as a builder. That's when you should be the most excited.
turns.zh: 现在，有许多其他公司显然是好的想法，你仍然可以在这些公司取得巨大成功，但如果想法是显而易见的，许多其他有雄心的人也会开始做。所以当我们在 2015 年创办 OpenAI 时，我想你可以用一只手数出那年成立的 AGI 实验室的数量。我的意思是，也许你可以用远少于一只手数出来。也许那一年只有 OpenAI。我不确定。然而可能有大约 1 万家照片分享公司。大多数人认为创办照片分享公司是更好的主意。但问题是有 1 万家其他公司，而且 Instagram 有巨大的网络效应等等。所以我认为选择那些你有理由相信比看起来更有价值的事情，即使它们不太可能成功。所以如果它们成功，价值很高，期望值很好。当你找到这样的东西时，你有真正的优势。当你比其他人更早理解一项技术或一门科学或世界的某些事情时，有一种本能，我理解，会说：‘啊，你知道，有这么多聪明人，我不想让他们说我傻，所以你不懂，他们会说服我放弃。’但我认为有另一种本能，我鼓励人们培养，那就是如果你真正理解某件事，而且不仅仅是一厢情愿的想法，但你能阐明为什么这是一个好赌注，你应该珍惜那些时刻。就像作为建设者，那太棒了。那是你应该最兴奋的时候。

turns.en: How do you decide that? How do you find a non-consensus bet?
turns.zh: 你如何决定？你如何找到非共识的赌注？

turns.en: Good question. I like my own experience of this was this was one thing that just no one ever taught me. And you know like very little of my experience in school was figuring out what questions to ask. You figure out how to answer other people's questions and then at some point I think like when you become a PhD student or whatever you get to start asking more questions and then eventually you do more and more of that. I think we should focus much more on teaching people, teaching very young people to figure out what questions to ask and what things are interesting to explore that we don't already know. And I think getting good at that skill was the best way that I figured out the sort of non-consensus bets to take.
turns.zh: 好问题。我自己的经验是，这是从来没有人教过我的事情。你知道，我在学校的经历很少是弄清楚该问什么问题。你学会回答别人的问题，然后到了某个时候，比如当你成为博士生之类的，你开始问更多问题，最终你做得越来越多。我认为我们应该更加注重教人们，教非常年轻的人弄清楚该问什么问题，以及哪些我们不知道的事情值得探索。我认为擅长这项技能是我找到那种非共识赌注的最佳方式。

turns.en: Just figuring out how to ask good questions.
turns.zh: 就是弄清楚如何问好问题。

turns.en: Figuring out how to ask good questions.
turns.zh: 弄清楚如何问好问题。

turns.en: Can you learn that?
turns.zh: 你能学会吗？

turns.en: I think so. Yeah. I mean like all of these things, maybe not everybody is going to have equal aptitude for everything, but I think this is one that a lot of people seem to be able to learn. You know, there's I forget which culture, which country has this rule where the kid when he comes back from school, the mother asks the kid that what's the question that you asked today?
turns.zh: 我认为可以。是的。我的意思是，像所有这些事情一样，也许不是每个人对每件事都有同等天赋，但我认为这是很多人似乎能够学会的。你知道，我忘了是哪种文化、哪个国家有这条规则，孩子放学回家时，母亲问孩子：你今天问了什么问题？

turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Do you know what culture? That's very interesting. You know what culture?
turns.zh: 你知道是什么文化吗？那很有趣。你知道是什么文化吗？

turns.en: I think it's Israel or something. Someone in Israel. I'm not sure but there is some culture where mothers just ask the kids they don't ask about the highlight they ask about the what's one question did you ask today.
turns.zh: 我想是以色列之类的。以色列的某个人。我不确定，但有一种文化，母亲只是问孩子，她们不问亮点，她们问的是：你今天问了什么问题？

turns.en: That's cool.
turns.zh: 那很酷。

turns.en: Is that a good habit that we
turns.zh: 这是一个好习惯吗，我们

turns.en: I'm going to start that with my kids. I'll report back in 15 years or something.
turns.zh: 我要开始对我的孩子这样做。我 15 年后左右会回来汇报。

turns.en: But how do you know that it's not wishful thinking? Is there a sign? Is there something that you can pin down and be like, 'Okay, if these are the signals in the thinking, the way I'm thinking, probably this makes sense'?
turns.zh: 但你怎么知道这不是一厢情愿？有迹象吗？有什么你可以确定并说‘好吧，如果这些是思考中的信号，我思考的方式，可能这有道理’？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean one thing is can you explain it to an optimistic, enthusiastic but kind of mentally disciplined smart friend and can you update them about why it might be a good bet? So, I remember when we were starting OpenAI, the default was like strongly skeptical, but I would talk to people and I would say, you know, here's the evidence. Here's what we've seen. Here's why this might work. Here's why it'd be huge if it worked. And here's why this is an approach that we think has legs and then, you know, if we can make superintelligence, it was kind of obvious why that would be valuable to make. And you know, not every time, but enough of the time when we talked to somebody who was like a smart person but a non-expert, they would say, 'Okay, that seems you can that updated me. That seems like it's worth doing.' Now, if we had convinced everybody, it probably would have been too obvious. But if we had not been able to convince anyone at all, I would have been more skeptical.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，一件事是你能向一个乐观、热情但思维上自律的聪明朋友解释它，并且你能让他们更新为什么这可能是一个好赌注吗？所以，我记得当我们创办 OpenAI 时，默认是强烈怀疑，但我会和人交谈，我会说，你知道，这是证据。这是我们看到的。这是为什么这可能有效。这是为什么如果它有效会巨大。这是为什么我们认为这种方法有潜力，然后，你知道，如果我们能制造超级智能，那为什么制造它有价值是显而易见的。而且你知道，不是每次，但足够多的时候，当我们和某个聪明但非专家的人交谈时，他们会说：‘好吧，那似乎——你让我更新了。那似乎值得做。’现在，如果我们说服了所有人，那可能太明显了。但如果我们根本无法说服任何人，我会更怀疑。

turns.en: Interesting. Now, as I'm saying that out loud, I'm thinking of there must be historical examples of where someone was not able to convince anyone and they were still right. So, at some point, you got to just like trust your own instincts here. Was there any point ever in your life where nobody else was convinced but just you?
turns.zh: 有趣。现在，当我大声说出来时，我在想一定有历史例子，有人无法说服任何人，但他们仍然是对的。所以，在某个时候，你只能相信自己的直觉。你生活中是否有过这样的时刻：除了你，没有人被说服？

turns.en: I mean, there have been like small decisions where I was like, 'Open I was going to do this thing and none of the rest of the leadership team wanted to.'
turns.zh: 我的意思是，有过一些小决定，比如‘公开——我打算做这件事，而领导团队的其他人都不想做。’

turns.en: Give me an example.
turns.zh: 给我一个例子。

turns.en: Um, launching ChatGPT was kind of an example of that. Not that people didn't want to launch a chatbot, but most people thought it was too early and not good enough.
turns.zh: 嗯，推出 ChatGPT 就是一个例子。并不是人们不想推出聊天机器人，但大多数人认为为时过早，而且不够好。

turns.en: Interesting. And what made you go against all of them and be like, 'Hey, let's just launch it'? The YC ground.
turns.zh: 有趣。是什么让你违背所有他们的意见，说‘嘿，我们就推出它吧’？YC 的磨砺。

turns.en: I think it was the Yeah, I think it was I think it was the YC experience. I think so. Like I had really I had spent so long drilling it into founders that if you're not a little embarrassed of your first version, you're waiting too long to launch because what you need is feedback. The another thing that I had cuz we had this like internal version and this actually a good insight. The retention was terrible of their internal version. I think it was like you know 5% or something of the first version of ChatGPT people would use and keep using. Now there's a bunch of reasons why it was bad data in the first place. We had better models, we had other interfaces. But many people would look at that and say you can't launch a product with 5% retention. That's terrible. And normally that's true. But then you would talk to those 5% of users and some of them like really loved it.
turns.zh: 我想是——是的，我想是 YC 的经历。我想是的。就像我真的花了很长时间向创始人灌输：如果你对第一个版本不感到有点尴尬，那说明你等得太久才推出，因为你需要的是反馈。另一件事是我有——因为我们有这个内部版本，这实际上是一个很好的洞察。内部版本的留存率很糟糕。我想大约是 5% 左右的人会使用并继续使用 ChatGPT 的第一个版本。现在有很多原因说明这首先是糟糕的数据。我们有更好的模型，我们有其他界面。但很多人会看着它说，你不能推出一个留存率 5% 的产品。那太糟糕了。通常这是真的。但然后你会和那 5% 的用户交谈，其中一些人真的很喜欢它。

turns.en: And there's this other YC learning, which is the more important thing for an initial project: a small number of people that really love something, not a lot of people that like it a little bit. And so although the retention numbers of the internal ChatGPT prototype were very low, the people who liked it really used it a lot and really liked it. And I thought that was a very good sign.
turns.zh: 还有另一个 YC 的经验，对于初始项目来说更重要的是：一小群真正热爱它的人，而不是很多只是有点喜欢它的人。所以尽管内部 ChatGPT 原型的留存数据很低，但喜欢它的人真的用得很多，也真的很喜欢它。我觉得这是一个非常好的信号。

turns.en: And the first thing you said was two different things, right? The first was being embarrassed. Like if you're not embarrassed about your first product, then you're too late, right? Are you okay with being embarrassed even today?
turns.zh: 你刚才说的第一点其实是两件不同的事，对吧？第一是感到尴尬。就像如果你对自己的第一个产品不感到尴尬，那你就太晚了，对吧？即使今天，你也能接受尴尬吗？

turns.en: Yes, you're okay with being misunderstood and you're okay with being embarrassed.
turns.zh: 是的，你能接受被误解，也能接受尴尬。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I mean, look, I want us to put out great products, but I'm happy for us to put out some early sketches to get feedback and learn, and not all of them will work. But nothing changes with the scale of your company now because enough users trust you for—
turns.zh: 我的意思是，听着，我希望我们推出伟大的产品，但我也乐意推出一些早期的草图来获取反馈和学习，不是所有都会成功。但公司现在的规模并没有改变什么，因为有足够多的用户信任你——

turns.en: I mean things that we put out to like all of the entire ChatGPT user base have to have like a high threshold and also now that companies—I mean this is like getting close to critical infrastructure, companies are really reliant on this—and so for enterprise products we ship there's like a very, very high bar. Okay. So now things have changed now.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们向整个 ChatGPT 用户群推出的东西必须有一个很高的门槛，而且现在公司——这已经接近关键基础设施了，公司非常依赖这个——所以我们发布的企业产品有一个非常非常高的标准。好吧。所以现在情况已经变了。

turns.en: But then we can still experiment with other—you know, I think hopefully you'll see us experiment with many new products. Some of which will really delight you and make it into the core experience, and some of which people will look at and say, you know, it seems cool in theory, but it doesn't really fit for me.
turns.zh: 但我们仍然可以尝试其他——你知道，我希望你们会看到我们尝试许多新产品。有些会真正让你惊喜并进入核心体验，有些人们看了会说，理论上很酷，但不太适合我。

turns.en: Interesting. And the other thing is we're talking about being misunderstood. Do you think you're still being misunderstood today?
turns.zh: 有意思。另外我们刚才在谈被误解。你觉得今天你仍然被误解吗？

turns.en: I think at this point most of the world looks at AI and says, okay, I believe this thing is going to happen. Now clearly it's not all popular. And I think our vision for the world and what we hope for how people will use this tool, this technology, is still not very well understood. But I think people at least understand AI is happening.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在大多数世人看着 AI 说，好吧，我相信这事会发生。显然它并非人人欢迎。我认为我们对世界的愿景，以及我们希望人们如何使用这个工具、这项技术，仍然没有被很好地理解。但至少人们明白 AI 正在发生。

turns.en: Okay. Interesting. Let's come back to you trying to do something extraordinary, right? And you taking bets on other people as well. And you're talking about YC, right? There's another quote which you have only written—I'm paraphrasing—and it's something like your will to bend reality or your will to bend the world. The percentage of that particular thing is really high. Most people don't even try. Something like that you said. Do you remember?
turns.zh: 好。有意思。让我们回到你尝试做非凡之事的话题，对吧？你也押注其他人。你在谈 YC，对吧？还有一句话，你只写过——我转述一下——大概是你的意志去弯曲现实或弯曲世界。那个特定东西的百分比很高。大多数人甚至不尝试。类似这样的话你说过。你记得吗？

turns.en: I remember something like this. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我记得类似的话。是的。

turns.en: Like most people don't even try.
turns.zh: 就像大多数人甚至不尝试。

turns.en: I think it's more like bending the reality. You can do it much more than you think, or people can do it much more than they think, and most people don't try enough. Something like that.
turns.zh: 我觉得更像是弯曲现实。你能做到的比你想象的多得多，或者人们能做的比他们想象的多得多，而大多数人尝试得不够。大概是这样。

turns.en: Yeah. And why do you think people don't take the moonshot?
turns.zh: 嗯。那你觉得为什么人们不采取登月行动？

turns.en: I have a bunch of theories on this, but many of them boil down to people want to stay part of the herd, and it's more comfortable to not do something unusual and maybe fail or maybe look wrong or maybe look dumb. And there's a real—it's easy to point to the evolutionary biology reasons of why this would be true, like you don't want to get kicked out of the tribe or whatever. But I think people have really strong pressures to not do that kind of stuff just because of the way society is built.
turns.zh: 我有很多理论，但很多归结为人们想留在群体中，不做不寻常的事更舒服，也许失败，也许看起来错了，也许看起来愚蠢。而且有真正的——很容易指出进化生物学的原因来解释为什么这是真的，比如你不想被踢出部落之类的。但我认为人们有非常强烈的压力不去做那种事，只是因为社会的构建方式。

turns.en: I mean, even more than that, I think society is built the way it is because of evolutionary pressure, and I think that's probably very deep for most of us.
turns.zh: 我是说，甚至不止如此，我认为社会之所以这样构建是因为进化压力，而且我认为这对我们大多数人来说可能根深蒂固。

turns.en: And what was in you? What was there in you which helped you bend this will or the world according to your will?
turns.zh: 那你内心有什么？你内心有什么帮助你弯曲这个意志或按照你的意志弯曲世界？

turns.en: I think like a lot of tech people I've always just had, which would be a negative in many other contexts, like a little bit less of whatever that internal pressure to stay on the track and do the same thing as other people. And I kind of think that's probably mostly a genetic thing.
turns.zh: 我觉得像很多科技人一样，我一直都有——这在许多其他情境下会是负面——就是少一点那种留在轨道上、和别人做同样事情的内部压力。我有点认为这主要是基因的事。

turns.en: Just genetic? You don't think there's any other thing that you're building?
turns.zh: 只是基因？你不认为还有其他你正在构建的东西吗？

turns.en: Oh, I'm sure there's other things, too. But you know, you can find all these studies about how people that are slightly autistic tend to be more likely to invent new science or just get obsessed with one idea and work super hard in the lab against all the odds for it.
turns.zh: 哦，我肯定还有其他东西。但你知道，你可以找到所有这些研究，关于轻微自闭的人往往更可能发明新科学，或者只是痴迷于一个想法，在实验室里不顾一切地超级努力。

turns.en: Yeah. And what was the will-bending moment for you?
turns.zh: 嗯。那对你来说，弯曲意志的时刻是什么？

turns.en: I mean, probably starting OpenAI. Like, hopefully—it's too early to say, but I think that'll probably be the most important thing I ever did.
turns.zh: 我是说，可能是创办 OpenAI。希望——现在说还太早，但我认为那可能是我做过的最重要的事。

turns.en: Do you worry about it?
turns.zh: 你担心它吗？

turns.en: About?
turns.zh: 担心什么？

turns.en: Yeah. About OpenAI?
turns.zh: 嗯。关于 OpenAI？

turns.en: Yeah, of course.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。

turns.en: What's your biggest worry?
turns.zh: 你最大的担忧是什么？

turns.en: I mean, we are going to do something—or we have done something—and will continue to do something that is going to be an extraordinary force in society. I believe it can be a force for good, and it will be a force for good on net, great good, but you know, it's very high stakes and we have a lot of responsibility.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们将要做一些事——或者已经做了一些事——并将继续做一些事，这将成为社会中一股非凡的力量。我相信它可以成为一股向善的力量，净效果将是向善的，巨大的善，但你知道，这风险极高，我们肩负着很大的责任。

turns.en: True. You know, this takes me to the point where you wrote an essay which was in the beginning about superintelligence. Yeah.
turns.zh: 确实。你知道，这让我想到你写的一篇文章，开头是关于超级智能的。嗯。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And after that essay, during that May, you wrote to Elon about it and you said something like it would be good if someone else apart from Google started it, right?
turns.zh: 在那篇文章之后，那年五月，你写信给 Elon 谈了这件事，你说如果除了 Google 之外还有别人启动它就好了，对吧？

turns.en: So you said like the biggest threat for continued human existence, the biggest threat is going to be superintelligence.
turns.zh: 所以你说，人类持续生存的最大威胁，最大的威胁将是超级智能。

turns.en: Right. Why do you think that if you started it makes less of a threat?
turns.zh: 对。为什么你认为如果你来启动它，威胁就会小一些？

turns.en: Well, I believe in pluralism. I don't think only us having it is good either. I think there are two kind of cartoonish ways this goes really wrong.
turns.zh: 嗯，我相信多元化。我也不认为只有我们拥有它是好事。我认为有两种相当卡通化的方式会让事情严重出错。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: One is that there's a loss of control to AI, and we intentionally or accidentally cede control of the future to systems that are unbelievably more capable than we are and we can't get it back. And the other is like one person or company or country gets way too powerful relative to everybody else. And I think that's very unstable. I think it'd actually be much better for the world for there to be multiple AI efforts with slightly different approaches that are competing with each other and putting out in different ways. And you know, we talked earlier about the dislike of powerful people. I also have this dislike of intense power concentration. I think that's not what works. So I'm hopeful we don't do that.
turns.zh: 一是对 AI 失去控制，我们有意或无意地把未来的控制权交给比我们强大得难以置信的系统，而且我们无法收回。另一个是某个人、公司或国家相对于其他所有人变得过于强大。我认为那非常不稳定。我认为对世界来说，有多个 AI 努力以略有不同的方法相互竞争并以不同方式推出，实际上会好得多。你知道，我们之前谈过不喜欢有权势的人。我也不喜欢权力过度集中。我认为那不是行之有效的方式。所以我希望我们不要那样做。

turns.en: So is that what you were thinking when you started it as well? That someone with all the means in the world should not get this power today.
turns.zh: 那么你创办它时也是这么想的吗？一个拥有世界上所有资源的人不应该在今天获得这种权力。

turns.en: Well, at least there shouldn't be one. Like you want I think many efforts.
turns.zh: 嗯，至少不应该只有一个。就像你希望我认为有很多努力。

turns.en: Okay. And let's say now there are like too many, right? There are four, five large companies. They have all the capital in the world. They have the great talent. They have all sorts of technology research. They all are working at it. What's your unfair advantage in this?
turns.zh: 好吧。假设现在有太多公司了，对吧？有四五家大公司。他们拥有世界上所有的资本。他们拥有顶尖人才。他们拥有各种技术研究。他们都在努力。你在这方面有什么不公平的优势？

turns.en: Um, I think we have, you know, the most users and the best stack from chips to data centers to models to other things that come around that um to to sort of put an abundant put abundant intelligence into people's hands. Uh I think we have the best brand and the sort of the values that people who are going to use this technology want. Like we want everybody else to succeed and I think people can feel that from us. We don't want to be like the one company to rule everybody. This goes back to our founding.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为我们拥有最多的用户，以及从芯片到数据中心到模型再到其他相关事物的最佳技术栈，嗯，从而将丰富的智能交到人们手中。呃，我认为我们拥有最好的品牌，以及那些将要使用这项技术的人们所想要的价值观。就像我们希望其他所有人都成功，我认为人们能从我们身上感受到这一点。我们不想成为统治所有人的那一家公司。这要追溯到我们的创立之初。

turns.en: No, I was talking about what makes you the Sam.
turns.zh: 不，我是在说是什么让你成为萨姆。

turns.en: Oh me personally.
turns.zh: 哦，我个人。

turns.en: What do you think is your super advantage?
turns.zh: 你认为你的超级优势是什么？

turns.en: Uh, well, I've been doing it the longest. I mean, I guess it's not true. I guess Dennis has been doing it longer than me. I I I think I have like a big advantage of just having had a lot of time to watch this development all the way through and not just for the intuitions about how to run the company, but connections throughout the whole ecosystem. Uh, they really helped there.
turns.zh: 呃，嗯，我做这行时间最长。我的意思是，我猜这并不正确。我猜丹尼斯做这行比我更久。我我我认为我有一个很大的优势，就是有大量时间从头到尾观察这个发展过程，不仅仅是关于如何运营公司的直觉，还有整个生态系统中的人脉。呃，这些真的很有帮助。

turns.en: Interesting. But you must be doing something right. You said not sure about how to run the company but you're doing something right about the company because when you were fired there were 700 people who threatened to resign. What do you think you did right as a founder that 700 people like almost the entire company is ready to back you?
turns.zh: 有趣。但你一定做对了什么。你说不确定如何运营公司，但你在公司方面做对了一些事情，因为当你被解雇时，有 700 人威胁要辞职。你认为作为创始人你做对了什么，让 700 人——几乎整个公司——都准备好支持你？

turns.en: Um I don't think it's any like one thing but and I don't think this is I don't think it's even mostly about me. I mean maybe the thing that I I did is I got to like you know pick the leadership team and sort of set up how we what we run at and how we how we work. But uh I think the thing that we have done most right is we've just built an extraordinary collection of people really motivated by the same mission um with a very healthy culture for the right combination of being sure and high conviction where we need to be that and being open-minded and exploratory everywhere else. And that that that is a special culture. I I I think like the someday when the history books get written on OpenAI, the thing that I hope they talk about the most is our rediscovery of the kind of culture that makes a great research lab and how why that had gone missing for so long.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不认为这是任何单一的事情，而且我不认为这甚至主要是关于我。我的意思是，也许我做的事情是我选择了领导团队，并设定了我们如何运营以及如何工作。但呃，我认为我们做得最对的事情是我们建立了一个非凡的人才集合，他们真正被同一个使命所驱动，嗯，拥有非常健康的文化，在需要自信和高信念的地方保持自信和高信念，在其他所有地方保持开放和探索。这这这是一种特殊的文化。我我我认为，当有一天关于 OpenAI 的历史书写成时，我最希望他们谈论的是我们重新发现了那种造就伟大研究实验室的文化，以及为什么这种文化缺失了那么久。

turns.en: And what can people learn from the culture that you've built here if someone is a young founder who's trying to build something like this?
turns.zh: 如果有人是一位年轻创始人，试图建立类似的东西，人们可以从你在这里建立的文化中学到什么？

turns.en: Um, one thing is having very high convictions, extreme clarity on what you are setting out to do. And even if what you set out to do, maybe even more so if what you set out to do sounds crazy to most people, the fact that you are willing to take that approach um to talk and think that way is very appealing to some set of people. And so when we started, we said we're going to try to build AGI and this is the direction that we're going to push in to try to get there. But the main thing is that like we have a bet on AGI and if our initial direction turns out to be wrong, we'll change. There were not many other efforts in the world that were still willing to say they were trying to build AGI. I think even Deep Mind at that point had stopped saying they were trying to do it. turns.en: There's many things that are a disaster: lack of drive, lack of focus, lack of clarity, lack of vision, lack of ability to solve hard problems repeatedly with a smile on your face. All of these things are anti-patterns. So there are many things that are almost certain to predict failure, but that part is easier.
turns.zh: 会酿成灾难的事情很多：缺乏驱动力、缺乏专注、缺乏清晰度、缺乏愿景、缺乏反复解决难题还能笑着面对的能力。这些都是反模式。所以，几乎必然预示失败的事情有很多，但那部分反而更容易。

turns.en: A lot of ways, different ways to succeed. You said the first thing is lack of drive.
turns.zh: 成功有很多种、不同的方式。你说第一点是缺乏驱动力。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And it's ambition, a lot of people talk about. Can you train somebody or can you teach somebody to be more ambitious?
turns.zh: 那就是野心，很多人都在谈。你能训练一个人、或者教一个人变得更有野心吗？

turns.en: Yes, I think you can. This was one of my most pleasant surprises of YC. And I think part of why YC adds much more value to the world than people realize is that there are some things that maybe you can't train, but you can teach people to become more ambitious. Not everybody. It's hard to predict who you'll be able to, but it can definitely happen.
turns.zh: 能，我觉得可以。这是我在 YC 最惊喜的发现之一。我觉得 YC 对世界的价值比人们意识到的要大，部分原因就在于：有些东西也许没法训练，但你可以教人变得更有野心。不是所有人，很难预测你能教会谁，但这确实会发生。

turns.en: How do you teach it?
turns.zh: 你怎么教？

turns.en: I found that the most successful thing was one, a combination of a peer group going through the same thing, and two, getting people to go through successive challenges at increasing difficulty and realizing that they can do more than they think, do more than they think, better instincts, and keep going.
turns.zh: 我发现最有效的做法是：第一，把一群经历相同的人组成同伴群体；第二，让人连续经历难度递增的挑战，让他们意识到自己能做得比自己以为的更多——做得更多、直觉更好，然后继续往前走。

turns.en: And did you become ambitious like this when you were in the same peer group, or were you ambitious from before?
turns.zh: 那你是进了这样的同伴群体之后才变得有野心的，还是之前就有野心？

turns.en: No, I think I got much more ambitious.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得我变得有野心多了。

turns.en: And do you think the ambition comes from confidence that everyone else around me is ambitious, or does it come from insecurity?
turns.zh: 你觉得这种野心是来自“我周围所有人都很有野心”带来的信心，还是来自不安全感？

turns.en: Paul Graham used to say that there was something about the pressure of demo day coming up and people not wanting to fail. And I think that's kind of a version of insecurity. But I think much more it comes from there's excitement and there's a positive force of being around these people doing these amazing things, and you're like, well, you know, we all entered this together and if they can do it, so can I.
turns.zh: Paul Graham 以前说过，Demo Day 临近带来的压力、以及人们不想失败，这里面有点东西。我觉得那算是一种不安全感。但我认为更多是来自兴奋感，来自和这些人一起做这些了不起的事情所产生的正向力量，你会想：我们都是一起进来的，他们能做到，我也能。

turns.en: For you, it's more confidence.
turns.zh: 对你来说，更多是信心。

turns.en: I think so. And I really think that if you keep getting slightly bigger, slightly bigger, slightly bigger challenges and keep excelling at them, you really do build a lot of successive confidence and learning.
turns.zh: 我想是的。而且我真的认为，如果你不断接到稍微大一点、再大一点、再大一点的挑战，并且一直把它们做好，你确实会积累起大量层层递进的信心和认知。

turns.en: Interesting. And is it only the peer circle of the group that makes you like this?
turns.zh: 有意思。那是不是只有同伴圈子才能让你变成这样？

turns.en: What do you mean?
turns.zh: 你是什么意思？

turns.en: Like, is it only that other ambitious people actually give you these things?
turns.zh: 就是，是不是只有其他有野心的人才能给你这些东西？

turns.en: No, I think you can get it lots of ways. But I think we as people are hardwired to learn from the people around us. There's that famous quote, which is like, you're going to become the average of your five best friends, so you better pick those five people really well.
turns.zh: 不是，我觉得获得它的方式有很多。但我认为人天生就会向身边的人学习。有句名言说，你会变成你最好的五个朋友的平均值，所以你最好把那五个人选好。

turns.en: You believe in it?
turns.zh: 你信这句话吗？

turns.en: Not quite, but there's some truth to it, obviously.
turns.zh: 不完全信，但显然有一定道理。

turns.en: What's the worst advice you've gotten as a founder?
turns.zh: 你作为创始人收到过的最糟糕的建议是什么？

turns.en: I mean, almost all the advice is terrible. I don't know how to pick the worst thing, but I would say my meta advice to founders is listen to less advice.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，几乎所有建议都很糟糕。我不知道怎么挑出最糟的，但我想说，我给创始人的元建议就是：少听建议。

turns.en: Listen to less advice.
turns.zh: 少听建议。

turns.en: Listen to less advice.
turns.zh: 少听建议。

turns.en: Do you sometimes go home at some point and be like, hey, all this advice is maybe right and maybe I'm wrong?
turns.zh: 你有时候回家会不会想：嘿，这些建议也许是对的，也许是我错了？

turns.en: I think YC could probably distill five to 10 very important, highly confident pieces of general advice from all of the incredible wealth of experience. And I think you should listen to those five or 10 things. Like I think the slogan of YC, or the motto, whatever it is, make something people want, that is like the single commandment of startup advice, to the degree there is one thing for early-stage startups. And then there's another list of things that are almost as important. But you're not going to become a great founder by listening to the 800th podcast of advice about how to start a startup. You've got to just do it and figure it out on your own. And a lot of the advice that you need is so specific to your case that beyond the axiomatic truths, there's not that much more to learn from one more podcast.
turns.zh: 我觉得 YC 大概能从海量经验里提炼出 5 到 10 条非常重要、把握很大的通用建议。你应该听的就是那 5 到 10 条。比如 YC 的口号——或者座右铭，随便怎么叫——“做出人们想要的东西”，这几乎就是创业建议的唯一戒律，至少对早期创业公司来说，如果只能有一条的话。然后还有另一串几乎同样重要的东西。但你不听第 800 期关于如何创业的播客，也不会因此成为伟大的创始人。你得直接去做，自己去摸索。而且你需要的很多建议都太针对你的具体情况了，除了那些公理级的真理之外，再听一期播客也学不到多少东西。

turns.zh: 嗯，我记得我写过。但我不记得内容是什么了。我敢打赌现在我能写出更好的版本，也能写出更短的版本。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: I think this point about compounding is the one I had first in there. I think this is probably underestimated. A lot of people don't drive themselves to continued forward progress. The joke is: sure, you have 20 years of experience, but you have 20 times the same one year of experience. The thing I think is so cool about a career is you can build on each successive phase, but you have to continue to push yourself. You have to keep doing uncomfortable, non-obvious new things. And a lot of people fall off that very early in their careers. So staying on the compounding exponential curve is empirically not what most people do. And I think that's a very good, non-obvious piece of advice.
turns.zh: 我认为关于复利这一点是我最先提到的。我觉得这很可能被低估了。很多人不会驱动自己持续向前进步。有个笑话是：当然，你有 20 年经验，但你是把同一年的经验重复了 20 次。我觉得职业生涯最酷的地方在于，你可以在每个 successive 阶段上构建，但你必须继续推动自己。你必须持续做不舒服、不显而易见的新事情。而很多人在职业生涯很早期就掉队了。所以，从经验上看，保持在复利指数曲线上并不是大多数人会做的事。我认为这是一条非常好、不显而易见的建议。

turns.zh: 你最近做的最不舒服的事情是什么？

turns.en: Most of the stuff now feels new again. Figuring out how we're going to navigate this current debate about pacing progress feels like a very difficult thing to get right and pretty important, and just yeah, hard and new.
turns.zh: 现在大多数事情感觉又都是新的了。弄清楚我们如何应对当前关于进展节奏的争论，感觉是一件非常难做对且相当重要的事情，而且是的，既困难又新鲜。

turns.zh: 那你怎么做来确保你做对呢？有没有什么

turns.en: A lot of time thinking and talking to people and trying to get more data and more new ideas into the mix.
turns.zh: 花很多时间思考、与人交谈，并尝试把更多数据和更多新想法纳入其中。

turns.en: Do you ever go home sometimes and be like, "Maybe I'm wrong about this."
turns.zh: 你有时候回家会不会想：“也许我在这件事上错了。”

turns.en: Yeah, of course. And I think it'd be disastrous if I didn't. We talk about conviction and self-belief and all of that. I think what some people take that to mean is don't introspect. Just be sure in what you're going to be sure and don't question it. I try to question everything all the time. I still try to act consistently and with conviction until I find a reason to change my mind. But I think this is really important.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我觉得如果我不这样想，那才是灾难性的。我们谈论信念、自信等等。我认为有些人把这理解为不要内省。只要对你将要确信的事情保持确信，不要质疑它。我试图一直质疑一切。我仍然试图保持一致并带着信念行动，直到找到改变主意的理由。但我认为这真的很重要。

turns.en: Give me an example. How do you do it?
turns.zh: 给我举个例子。你是怎么做的？

turns.en: My process often is just to keep thinking about the same question from every different angle, throwing out a bunch of bad ideas, trying to break them apart or find problems with them in my own head, then going to other people. Taking more input, trying a different version of it out, adapting it again. I think it's an iterative process like that.
turns.zh: 我的过程通常是不断从各个不同角度思考同一个问题，抛出一堆糟糕的想法，试图在我自己的头脑中拆解它们或找出问题，然后去找其他人。吸收更多输入，尝试不同的版本，再次调整。我认为这就是一个迭代的过程。

turns.en: Like give me an example of this. Like would you let's say what's your current big problem and then you're just questioning from different angles and
turns.zh: 比如给我举个例子。比如你当前的大问题是什么，然后你只是从不同角度质疑，并且

turns.en: I think the one that I just gave, this question of how do we think about the pace of progress as we enter this RSI era and how do we avoid these two ways that things could go wrong, either from a loss of control incident or a concentration of power incident, and what is the right governance mechanism, how do we think about how smart an AI system should be allowed to be relative to a person. How quickly can that improve? How do we think about the questions around security and monitoring and alignment, and where can we afford to take risks and not.
turns.zh: 我想就是我刚才提到的那个问题：当我们进入 RSI 时代，我们如何看待进步的速度，以及我们如何避免两种可能出错的方式——要么是失去控制的事件，要么是权力集中事件，正确的治理机制是什么，我们如何看待一个 AI 系统相对于一个人应该被允许有多聪明。它能多快改进？我们如何看待安全、监控和 alignment 相关的问题，以及我们在哪里可以承担风险，哪里不能。

turns.en: And does that change when you're at home? Because when you're at home
turns.zh: 那你在家的时候会改变吗？因为当你在家时

turns.zh: 是的。

turns.zh: 你看到你的孩子，看到你的家人，你可能会想，好吧，也许我从不同的视角思考。

turns.en: I am a big—I mean when I'm with my kids I try to just hang out with my kids and be the best dad I can be and I try not to get myself distracted thinking about other stuff. But I have noticed a big difference on the weekend mornings when I'm working at home versus in the office. And I am a real believer, for me at least, that finding some sort of rhythm where you can intensely be with people and working very interactively and then have real chunks of time where you can shut out the world and just think and work on your own. That back and forth rhythm is super important to my particular style.
turns.zh: 我非常——我的意思是，当我和孩子们在一起时，我尽量只是和他们待在一起，做最好的爸爸，尽量不让自己分心去想其他事情。但我注意到周末早上在家工作与在办公室工作有很大不同。我坚信，至少对我而言，找到某种节奏，让你可以高强度地与人相处、非常互动地工作，然后有真正的大块时间可以屏蔽世界，独自思考和工作。这种来回的节奏对我的特定风格非常重要。

turns.en: You can do that easily or you have to learn hard way.
turns.zh: 你能轻松做到这一点，还是必须通过艰难的方式学习？

turns.en: Yeah, that's just what works for me. It's very natural and easy.
turns.zh: 是的，这只是适合我的方式。它非常自然和容易。

turns.zh: 关闭并屏蔽，就像只是

turns.en: Shutting down. It's just like a very different way of working. Like when I'm working at my office at home, it's like a very solo style of work. And if I only did that, it would be a disaster. But if I didn't have that and only was like constantly in meetings at the office, that also wouldn't work for me. So I need that back and forth.
turns.zh: 关闭。这就像一种非常不同的工作方式。比如当我在家中的办公室工作时，那是一种非常独处的工作风格。如果我只这样做，那会是灾难。但如果我没有这种独处，只是不断在办公室开会，那对我也不可行。所以我需要那种来回。

turns.en: Yeah, I think it—I mean as I said earlier there's all these ways it could go wrong and so I don't know what the future's going to look like but I am comfortable that I have enormous trust in people to figure out how to adapt and thrive and make society better for all of us and yeah I think the world will most likely keep getting much better.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为——我的意思是，正如我之前所说，有所有这些可能出错的方式，所以我不知道未来会是什么样子，但我感到安心的是，我非常信任人们能够弄清楚如何适应和繁荣，并让社会对我们所有人更好，而且是的，我认为世界最有可能继续变得更好。

turns.zh: 而那是你想建造的东西。
